I. INTRODUCTION
A. Background and Related Works
Driven by widespread Internet of Things (IoT) applications such as smart trafﬁc and factory
automation, ultra-massive machine type communication (umMTC) is expected to be a primary
use case in future wireless networks. A key challenge in umMTC scenarios is to enable efﬁcient
and reliable random access for large numbers of devices, among which only a small fraction
are active and transmit a relatively small amount of information to the base-station (BS) [2].
In traditional grant-based random access protocols, active users wait for the grant of dedicated
transmission resources from the BS, leading to prolonged latency and reduced spectral efﬁciency.
Consequently, several grant-free random access schemes have been proposed where active users
are allowed to simultaneously access wireless networks without waiting for a grant [3]–[5].
Given that each user becomes active in an intermittent pattern and accesses the network without
a grant, the number of active users is typically random and unknown to the receiver [6].
A brief comparison between information-theoretic results on random access is summarized in
Table I. In a grant-free scenario, a commonly adopted approach is to assign each potential user a
unique pilot for user identiﬁcation. Each active user transmits its pilot followed by a message. The
classical information-theoretic treatment of such a scheme assumes each user has an individual
codebook. Several attempts to explore fundamental limits of random access with individual
codebooks can be found in [7]–[10]. However, in scenarios with large numbers of potential
users, such as umMTC, designing and allocating a unique pilot or codebook to each user may
impose a signiﬁcant burden on the system. It is also overly wasteful since many users may remain

The above theoretical results have been established under the assumption of knowing the
number of active users in advance. This assumption implies that the receiver has prior knowledge
of the sparsity level when treating data detection as a sparse support recovery problem. However,
this assumption is overoptimistic in practically relevant random access channels. This is because
users typically have intermittent or bursty communication patterns and access the network without
a grant, thereby leading to variations in the number of active users over time. To this end,
Yavas et al. [16] explored a URA scenario with a ﬁxed and unknown number of active users,
and derived an achievability bound on the error probability applying variable-length codes and
feedback. This bound was improved in [17] by using random codewords uniformly distributed
on a sphere and a maximum likelihood (ML) decoder. In the case of Ka = O(1), the proposed
Gaussian random-access code was proved to achieve the same third-order performance as the best

5
known result for Gaussian multiple-access with known user activity [17]. Assuming the number
of active users is random and unknown, a random-access code accounting for both misdetection
and false-alarm probabilities was deﬁned in [6]. On the basis of this code, achievability and
converse bounds on the two probabilities were derived for Gaussian channels, where the converse
bound is an ensemble converse bound and is speciﬁc to a scheme where the BS ﬁrst estimates
the number of active users and then chooses the number of returned messages in an interval
around the estimated value. For point-to-point (P2P) channels, non-asymptotic bounds on the
maximum coding rate were established in [18]. Moreover, the authors in [19] analyzed estimation
performance of the number of active users in single-receive-antenna fading channels, where active
users are required to transmit a common sequence before message. However, allocating additional
channel uses for the transmission of a common sequence may result in lower spectral efﬁciency.
Despite these existing results, the fundamental limits of URA with a random and unknown
number of active users are still not well understood. First, when each active user randomly
transmits a codeword from a common codebook over fading channels, the estimation performance
of the number of active users remains unclear, and how the lack of knowledge of the sparsity
level affects data detection performance remains uncertain. Second, most existing results related
to URA with an unknown sparsity level are conﬁned to the setting with a single-antenna receiver.
In the case where the BS is equipped with multiple antennas, it is unclear how the minimum
required energy-per-bit behaves when each active user transmits a ﬁxed number of bits using
ﬁnite channel uses. Third, in the asymptotic regime with a random and unknown number of
active users, the scaling behavior of the statistics of the number of active users, blocklength,
power, and number of BS antennas is unclear. This work aims to address these issues in both
non-asymptotic and asymptotic regimes applying information-theoretic tools.

### **Core Innovation**

The paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing the fundamental limits of unsourced random access (URA) in MIMO quasi-static Rayleigh fading channels with a random and unknown number of active users. The key innovation lies in deriving non-asymptotic achievability and converse bounds on the minimum energy-per-bit required for reliable communication, considering both misdetection and false-alarm probabilities. The framework reveals that the energy efficiency improves as the number of receive antennas (L) and the expected number of active users (E[Ka]) increase, with the error requirement becoming milder as these parameters grow.

### **Technical Approach**

1. **Energy-Based Estimation**: The paper employs an energy-based estimator to estimate the number of active users (Ka) based on the received signal (Y). This estimator is used to derive bounds on the misdetection and false-alarm probabilities.
2. **Non-Asymptotic Bounds**: The authors derive non-asymptotic achievability and converse bounds on the minimum energy-per-bit required for reliable URA. These bounds are applicable to systems with finite blocklength and are derived under the assumption of a random and unknown number of active users.
3. **Converse Bounds**: The paper also derives converse bounds on the error probability for URA, which provide a lower bound on the achievable rate given the number of active users and the blocklength.
4. **Simulation Results**: The authors validate their theoretical findings through extensive simulations, demonstrating the performance of the proposed bounds in practical scenarios.

### **Quantitative Findings**

1. **Non-Asymptotic Bounds**: The derived non-asymptotic bounds show that the probability of misdetection and false-alarm decreases exponentially with the number of receive antennas (L) and the expected number of active users (E[Ka]). The bounds also reveal that the error probability reaches a plateau as the power (P) and blocklength (n) increase, indicating a tradeoff between energy efficiency and reliability.
2. **Asymptotic Scaling Laws**: In the asymptotic regime, the paper establishes scaling laws on the minimum required power (P) and number of receive antennas (L) to reliably support Ka active users as functions of the blocklength (n). These scaling laws highlight the potential of MIMO in enabling low-cost communication and indicate that the minimum required power and number of receive antennas remain on the same order when the number of active users increases but stays below a threshold.
3. **Energy Efficiency**: The simulation results demonstrate that the extra required energy-per-bit due to the uncertainty in the number of active users decreases as L and E[Ka] increase and the error requirement becomes milder.

### **Limitations & Assumptions**

1. **Assumption of Random Sparsity**: The paper assumes that the number of active users is random and unknown, which may not hold in practical scenarios where users have intermittent or bursty communication patterns.
2. **Single-Antenna Receiver**: The analysis is primarily focused on single-receive-antenna channels, and the results for MIMO channels are derived under the assumption of a fixed number of active users.
3. **Fixed Channel Parameters**: The paper assumes fixed channel parameters, such as the number of transmit antennas and the blocklength, and does not consider the impact of dynamic channel conditions on the fundamental limits of URA.

### **Domain Impact**

1. **Theoretical Impact**: The paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the fundamental limits of URA in MIMO quasi-static Rayleigh fading channels, revealing the tradeoff between energy efficiency and reliability. The derived bounds and scaling laws offer a theoretical foundation for understanding the limits of URA and guide the design of practical URA schemes.
2. **Practical Impact**: The paper's findings are relevant for the design of URA architectures in future wireless networks, such as IoT and factory automation, where large numbers of devices with intermittent activity need to be supported. The results also highlight the potential of MIMO in enabling low-cost and energy-efficient communication in URA scenarios.

### **Key Equations and Figures**

of the sparsity level when treating data detection as a sparse support recovery problem. However,
this assumption is overoptimistic in practically relevant random access channels. This is because
users typically have intermittent or bursty communication patterns and access the network without
a grant, thereby leading to variations in the number of active users over time. To this end,
Yavas et al. [16] explored a URA scenario with a ﬁxed and unknown number of active users,
and derived an achievability bound on the error probability applying variable-length codes and
feedback. This bound was improved in [17] by using random codewords uniformly distributed
on a sphere and a maximum likelihood (ML) decoder. In the case of Ka = O(1), the proposed
Gaussian random-access code was proved to achieve the same third-order performance as the best

known result for Gaussian multiple-access with known user activity [17]. Assuming the number
of active users is random and unknown, a random-access code accounting for both misdetection
and false-alarm probabilities was deﬁned in [6]. On the basis of this code, achievability and
converse bounds on the two probabilities were derived for Gaussian channels, where the converse
bound is an ensemble converse bound and is speciﬁc to a scheme where the BS ﬁrst estimates
the number of active users and then chooses the number of returned messages in an interval
around the estimated value. For point-to-point (P2P) channels, non-asymptotic bounds on the
maximum coding rate were established in [18]. Moreover, the authors in [19] analyzed estimation
performance of the number of active users in single-receive-antenna fading channels, where active
users are required to transmit a common sequence before message. However, allocating additional
channel uses for the transmission of a common sequence may result in lower spectral efﬁciency.
Despite these existing results, the fundamental limits of URA with a random and unknown
number of active users are still not well understood. First, when each active user randomly
transmits a codeword from a common codebook over fading channels, the estimation performance
of the number of active users remains unclear, and how the lack of knowledge of the sparsity
level affects data detection performance remains uncertain. Second, most existing results related
to URA with an unknown sparsity level are conﬁned to the setting with a single-antenna receiver.
In the case where the BS is equipped with multiple antennas, it is unclear how the minimum
required energy-per-bit behaves when each active user transmits a ﬁxed number of bits using
ﬁnite channel uses. Third, in the asymptotic regime with a random and unknown number of
active users, the scaling behavior of the statistics of the number of active users, blocklength,
power, and number of BS antennas is unclear. This work aims to address these issues in both
non-asymptotic and asymptotic regimes applying information-theoretic tools.
B. Main Contributions
In this work, we explore the fundamental limits of URA in MIMO quasi-static Rayleigh fading
channels with random and unknown numbers of active users. To cope with the uncertainty in the
sparsity level, we estimate the number of active users and analyze the estimation performance in
both non-asymptotic and asymptotic regimes. Then, we delve into the data detection problem.
We derive non-asymptotic achievability and converse bounds to explore the fundamental tradeoff
among the payload size J, blocklength n, transmitting power P, number Ka of active users,
number L of BS antennas, and per-user probabilities of misdetection and false-alarm. The

6
achievability and converse bounds under the criterion of joint error probability are also discussed.
The derived ﬁnite-blocklength results play a crucial role in revealing the fundamental limits
of URA with stringent latency and energy constraints, and provide benchmarks to evaluate
practical schemes. In the asymptotic regime, we establish scaling laws to capture the underlying
relationship among system parameters. Moreover, we present extensive simulation results and
draw insightful conclusions from them. The contributions of this paper are as follows.
